remote_mcp.description: Deterministically recall whole-book concept and entity candidates with match reasons, bounded previews, and complete occurrence LIDs. Video graph candidates also retain distinct object meanings, text/visual/joint support, relations and video.read_frames hints. Read chosen text with book_text and actual video frames before citing. Read chosen occurrence LIDs with book_text and video_graph.read_hints with video.read_frames; pure visual objects have no invented LIDs.  Returns a built projection in data, not a generated answer. Collections are paged: data_path identifies a continuation's collection in the original projection and total_items its size. next_calls may include multiple collection branches and search batches. Concept matched_count/truncated still describe bounded candidate recall. Read chosen evidence LIDs with book_text. Missing built capability returns material_unavailable. Copy published_book_ref from book_list and check its available_tools. Costs 1 call on success, including empty results, each continuation page and repeated successful requests; failures cost 0. complete=false means more pages exist; copy needed next_calls name and arguments unchanged. sources gives published_book_ref, start_lid/end_lid, source_range and source_url: cite only evidence actually read, retaining its version and exact range. An empty sources array provides no source citation. usage is the server's post-call balance with charged_units and charged_from; do not infer balance locally. On quota_exhausted stop content retries and report usage.free_resets_at plus top_up_url or top_up_instruction; book_list and mcp_usage remain free.

resident.description: Use this accepted board when a visual relationship helps the current request. A short explanation, correction or clarification can be answered directly without authoring a diagram. Prioritize the host-selected explanation block over the rest of a long previous answer. When drawing is useful, read the relevant board layout and exact sources. Call plan with the concrete relationship before preparing new visuals or changing the explanation strategy; consume its coach handoff in the next sampling before drawing. Plan is run-local and reused by later prepare/revise/preview calls. Layout, font or position-only adjustments do not need a new plan. Search catalog or workspace.records.read only when relevant existing material or original conversations are needed. catalog searches all permitted sources before returning a bounded page; source_read returns an exact original snapshot and prepare imports resolves that same source identity. Workspace notes use kind note and stable note_id; their current text and shared relations are resolved from workspace.notes. Use workspace.notes relation_save to connect two note cards with a label and reason, never a duplicate native board link. Projected note_relation_id links are read-only and cannot be route/mapping targets. State the current learning workspace scope and never fabricate history or understanding. Choose the visual structure that explains the requested relationship. Use native drawings with text, shapes, paths and labelled links for flowcharts, causal networks, comparisons, spatial groupings and other freeform diagrams; circle/highlight with paths; connect explanations to visuals with mappings and progressive focus/reveal routes. Update existing native drawings through update_drawings and retained geometry through layout while keeping original answers and learner quotes immutable. Read the accepted persistent board, prepare native drawings with stable explanation blocks and a local teaching route, inspect the real Reader BoardCanvas preview, then stage exactly that observed candidate for the final successful answer. read returns the reserved answer item ID, current content revision and exact retained knowledge/understanding snapshots. Each prepare replaces the candidate and invalidates its preview. New content references use base_board_revision+1; existing references retain their exact observed revision. Every explanation block has an explicit stable block_id; never infer blocks from Markdown positions. Cite new source claims only with this turn's observed source.present references. Drawing based_on references identify formal conditions or actual learner evidence; they do not establish mastery. Do not fabricate learner quotes or understanding records; use tutor.step evidence for real user expressions. Preview images must be inspected in a later model sampling before deliver. Use commit to publish one complete observed part and keep working. A committed part survives cancellation or failure; read returns its exact receipts and the next reserved answer item ID. After any parts are committed, explicitly commit every additional part and finish with references to the saved parts. Deliver keeps the whole-turn staging path only when no parts have been committed. If the board changes, read and prepare/preview again. Existing presentations use declared real anchor IDs and exact PresentationRef; this tool never changes their experimental state. Board source citations: Substantive claims about the book, including its rules, conditions and specific values, require clickable original-source citations in direct text answers, explanation blocks and each committed part. Read the relevant book/library evidence in this turn and call source.present with the supporting observed passage. Then place [[source:<source_ref_id>]] after the supported sentence or closely related group of claims, using the exact returned ID; calling source.present alone does not attach a citation. Put these markers in blocks[].markdown before prepare/revise, so the saved explanation blocks and committed parts retain clickable sources. A derivation must identify its cited source premises and distinguish the inference from the author's statement. Label learner assumptions and illustrative values as such; they are not book evidence. Historical source_ref_ids and retained source_bindings are not this turn's evidence: reacquire support for new book claims, and cite only the references actually supporting the current explanation. If a required claim has no supporting observed passage, state the gap or narrow the claim; never invent a citation. Greetings, interface operations and layout-only changes need no forced citation. A concise recap may reuse clear nearby citations without repeating them. Compose around a clear visual model using shapes, spatial groups and labelled links. Give related nodes consistent alignment, generous whitespace and a small muted color palette. Keep node headings short and supporting text sparse; allocate enough space for ordinary headings around 22-26 px and body text around 16-19 px at natural scale. Put long explanations in blocks instead of shrinking text to cram the whole board onto one screen. Use local route focus to make each group readable while preserving the full model's relationships. Inspect hierarchy, spacing and readable text in the real preview. Continue revising only to fix a concrete wrong relationship, overlap, unreadable text or missing requested meaning; once those issues are resolved, deliver the inspected candidate. revise changes only the supplied existing blocks by block_id and drawings by item_id in the current uncommitted candidate, preserving every other item, link, mapping and route. Supply at least one change. It creates a new revision and invalidates the previous preview and teaching approval. Read collection=candidate_blocks for the original source-bound blocks. Preview and inspect the revised candidate before selecting it by move.board_candidate_revision; never rewrite its teaching body at select. For an explicitly requested mind map or a genuinely hierarchical outline, use operations create_mind_map and insert_topic with short topic titles and based_on references. Only these topics have derived tree edges and geometry. Freeform diagrams use drawings, links and explicit positions; drawings are full diagram content, not limited to annotations. Choose the form from the user request and the relationship being explained, not from whether a mind map already exists on the board. Both forms can coexist. Preserve the existing map and unrelated items when adding a different diagram. Reorganizing old drawings into a new mind map still requires the existing conversion confirmation. A selected topic scopes edits to that topic and descendants. Explanation or clarification requests may be answered as text only; expand, add an example, simplify or reorganize uses semantic operations without replacing unrelated branches. Use stable IDs and put_link/put_mapping/put_route to update existing relationships rather than duplicate them. On an unrelated human edit, read or preview rebases the existing candidate, changes its candidate_revision, and clears earlier preview and teaching approval. Inspect the new actual preview and repeat active teaching selection. On candidate_pending_changes, preserve the human result and offer to redo from current content; do not recreate deleted targets or overwrite the conflicting branch. Ordinary topic layout accepts no model coordinates except a new map's root anchor.

blocks.description: The explanation needed for this request and this visual relationship. Attach this turn's returned [[source:<source_ref_id>]] markers to substantive book claims in markdown; source.present calls without markers do not create clickable citations. Explain how to read the new visual or resolve the selected point; do not repeat the previous full answer merely to attach a diagram. Keep prose here and map it to concise visual nodes.

graphic.description: Text and shape labels support the same math delimiters as explanation blocks: $...$, $$...$$, \(...\), \[...\]. Write valid LaTeX, e.g. \(S_t = S_{t-1} + k_t v_t^{\mathsf T}\); avoid bare pseudo-math such as S_(t-1).

text.description: A concise node heading followed by a few short supporting lines. Let the shape and its links carry the visual model; move long prose to blocks.

points.description: Local coordinates within this drawing's size, relative to its position. Canvas coordinates equal position + point. For a circle around another item, place the path's position at the circle bounds and points around 0..width / 0..height; do not repeat absolute canvas coordinates.

avoid_when: Available for an accepted whole-board request or exact item focus, including blank boards. Keep retained answers and learner quotations immutable; edit mind-map topics through atomic operations and update free drawings or retained layout explicitly. A selected topic limits changes to its subtree. Never invent history, understanding or mastery; inspect the real candidate before publishing.
routing_card.description: Use this accepted board when a visual relationship helps the current request. A short explanation, correction or clarification can be answered directly without authoring a diagram. Prioritize the host-selected explanation block over the rest of a long previous answer. When drawing is useful, read the relevant board layout and exact sources. Call plan with the concrete relationship before preparing new visuals or changing the explanation strategy; consume its coach handoff in the next sampling before drawing. Plan is run-local and reused by later prepare/revise/preview calls. Layout, font or position-only adjustments do not need a new plan. Search catalog or workspace.records.read only when relevant existing material or original conversations are needed. catalog searches all permitted sources before returning a bounded page; source_read returns an exact original snapshot and prepare imports resolves that same source identity. Workspace notes use kind note and stable note_id; their current text and shared relations are resolved from workspace.notes. Use workspace.notes relation_save to connect two note cards with a label and reason, never a duplicate native board link. Projected note_relation_id links are read-only and cannot be route/mapping targets. State the current learning workspace scope and never fabricate history or understanding. Choose the visual structure that explains the requested relationship. Use native drawings with text, shapes, paths and labelled links for flowcharts, causal networks, comparisons, spatial groupings and other freeform diagrams; circle/highlight with paths; connect explanations to visuals with mappings and progressive focus/reveal routes. Update existing native drawings through update_drawings and retained geometry through layout while keeping original answers and learner quotes immutable. Read the accepted persistent board, prepare native drawings with stable explanation blocks and a local teaching route, inspect the real Reader BoardCanvas preview, then stage exactly that observed candidate for the final successful answer. read returns the reserved answer item ID, current content revision and exact retained knowledge/understanding snapshots. Each prepare replaces the candidate and invalidates its preview. New content references use base_board_revision+1; existing references retain their exact observed revision. Every explanation block has an explicit stable block_id; never infer blocks from Markdown positions. Cite new source claims only with this turn's observed source.present references. Drawing based_on references identify formal conditions or actual learner evidence; they do not establish mastery. Do not fabricate learner quotes or understanding records; use tutor.step evidence for real user expressions. Preview images must be inspected in a later model sampling before deliver. Use commit to publish one complete observed part and keep working. A committed part survives cancellation or failure; read returns its exact receipts and the next reserved answer item ID. After any parts are committed, explicitly commit every additional part and finish with references to the saved parts. Deliver keeps the whole-turn staging path only when no parts have been committed. If the board changes, read and prepare/preview again. Existing presentations use declared real anchor IDs and exact PresentationRef; this tool never changes their experimental state. Board source citations: Substantive claims about the book, including its rules, conditions and specific values, require clickable original-source citations in direct text answers, explanation blocks and each committed part. Read the relevant book/library evidence in this turn and call source.present with the supporting observed passage. Then place [[source:<source_ref_id>]] after the supported sentence or closely related group of claims, using the exact returned ID; calling source.present alone does not attach a citation. Put these markers in blocks[].markdown before prepare/revise, so the saved explanation blocks and committed parts retain clickable sources. A derivation must identify its cited source premises and distinguish the inference from the author's statement. Label learner assumptions and illustrative values as such; they are not book evidence. Historical source_ref_ids and retained source_bindings are not this turn's evidence: reacquire support for new book claims, and cite only the references actually supporting the current explanation. If a required claim has no supporting observed passage, state the gap or narrow the claim; never invent a citation. Greetings, interface operations and layout-only changes need no forced citation. A concise recap may reuse clear nearby citations without repeating them. Compose around a clear visual model using shapes, spatial groups and labelled links. Give related nodes consistent alignment, generous whitespace and a small muted color palette. Keep node headings short and supporting text sparse; allocate enough space for ordinary headings around 22-26 px and body text around 16-19 px at natural scale. Put long explanations in blocks instead of shrinking text to cram the whole board onto one screen. Use local route focus to make each group readable while preserving the full model's relationships. Inspect hierarchy, spacing and readable text in the real preview. Continue revising only to fix a concrete wrong relationship, overlap, unreadable text or missing requested meaning; once those issues are resolved, deliver the inspected candidate. revise changes only the supplied existing blocks by block_id and drawings by item_id in the current uncommitted candidate, preserving every other item, link, mapping and route. Supply at least one change. It creates a new revision and invalidates the previous preview and teaching approval. Read collection=candidate_blocks for the original source-bound blocks. Preview and inspect the revised candidate before selecting it by move.board_candidate_revision; never rewrite its teaching body at select. For an explicitly requested mind map or a genuinely hierarchical outline, use operations create_mind_map and insert_topic with short topic titles and based_on references. Only these topics have derived tree edges and geometry. Freeform diagrams use drawings, links and explicit positions; drawings are full diagram content, not limited to annotations. Choose the form from the user request and the relationship being explained, not from whether a mind map already exists on the board. Both forms can coexist. Preserve the existing map and unrelated items when adding a different diagram. Reorganizing old drawings into a new mind map still requires the existing conversion confirmation. A selected topic scopes edits to that topic and descendants. Explanation or clarification requests may be answered as text only; expand, add an example, simplify or reorganize uses semantic operations without replacing unrelated branches. Use stable IDs and put_link/put_mapping/put_route to update existing relationships rather than duplicate them. On an unrelated human edit, read or preview rebases the existing candidate, changes its candidate_revision, and clears earlier preview and teaching approval. Inspect the new actual preview and repeat active teaching selection. On candidate_pending_changes, preserve the human result and offer to redo from current content; do not recreate deleted targets or overwrite the conflicting branch. Ordinary topic layout accepts no model coordinates except a new map's root anchor.

match_mode.description: exact (default) matches unchanged text; normalized applies NFKC, full non-Turkic case folding and whitespace collapsing. Both locate literal occurrences, not semantic equivalents; result ranges use original-source UTF-16 positions.

order.description: document (default) returns earliest occurrences first; reverse_document returns latest first. Uses canonical source order, not lexical LID sorting. Combine before with reverse_document for previous occurrences.

page_size.description: Maximum literal occurrences per search page, 1..50, default 20. Does not change total_occurrences or exhaustive coverage of the requested literal scope; preserve it when using cursor.

query.description: Literal text to locate in canonical source, containing non-whitespace text and at most 4,096 Unicode scalar values. Exact mode preserves query whitespace; this is not a semantic question or regex. Read chosen hits using their start_lid/end_lid.

direction.description: before keeps hits ending at or before the reference span's start; after keeps hits starting at or after its end. Direction filters scope independently of result order.

lid.description: Known reference LID in this book. The relative filter excludes this node's entire source span, including its descendants.

relative_to.description: Optional before/after filter around a known LID, excluding that node's span. Intersects with within_lid when both are supplied.

within_lid.description: Known LID whose source span, including descendants, must contain each whole hit. Omit or null for no subtree restriction.

cursor.description: Opaque next_cursor from the preceding search result. Omit or null for the first page; preserve query, match_mode, scope, order and page_size on continuation. A changed source revision invalidates it.

match_mode.description: exact (default) matches unchanged text; normalized applies NFKC, full non-Turkic case folding and whitespace collapsing. Both locate literal occurrences, not semantic equivalents; result ranges use original-source UTF-16 positions.

order.description: document (default) returns earliest occurrences first; reverse_document returns latest first. Uses canonical source order, not lexical LID sorting. Combine before with reverse_document for previous occurrences.

page_size.description: Maximum literal occurrences per search page, 1..50, default 20. Does not change total_occurrences or exhaustive coverage of the requested literal scope; preserve it when using cursor.

query.description: Literal text to locate in canonical source, containing non-whitespace text and at most 4,096 Unicode scalar values. Exact mode preserves query whitespace; this is not a semantic question or regex. Read chosen hits using their start_lid/end_lid.

direction.description: before keeps hits ending at or before the reference span's start; after keeps hits starting at or after its end. Direction filters scope independently of result order.

cursor.description: Opaque next_cursor from the preceding search result. Omit or null for the first page; preserve query, match_mode, scope, order and page_size on continuation. A changed source revision invalidates it.

match_mode.description: exact (default) matches unchanged text; normalized applies NFKC, full non-Turkic case folding and whitespace collapsing. Both locate literal occurrences, not semantic equivalents; result ranges use original-source UTF-16 positions.

order.description: document (default) returns earliest occurrences first; reverse_document returns latest first. Uses canonical source order, not lexical LID sorting. Combine before with reverse_document for previous occurrences.

page_size.description: Maximum literal occurrences per search page, 1..50, default 20. Does not change total_occurrences or exhaustive coverage of the requested literal scope; preserve it when using cursor.

query.description: Literal text to locate in canonical source, containing non-whitespace text and at most 4,096 Unicode scalar values. Exact mode preserves query whitespace; this is not a semantic question or regex. Read chosen hits using their start_lid/end_lid.

direction.description: before keeps hits ending at or before the reference span's start; after keeps hits starting at or after its end. Direction filters scope independently of result order.

cursor.description: Opaque next_cursor from the preceding search result. Omit or null for the first page; preserve query, match_mode, scope, order and page_size on continuation. A changed source revision invalidates it.

match_mode.description: exact (default) matches unchanged text; normalized applies NFKC, full non-Turkic case folding and whitespace collapsing. Both locate literal occurrences, not semantic equivalents; result ranges use original-source UTF-16 positions.

order.description: document (default) returns earliest occurrences first; reverse_document returns latest first. Uses canonical source order, not lexical LID sorting. Combine before with reverse_document for previous occurrences.

page_size.description: Maximum literal occurrences per search page, 1..50, default 20. Does not change total_occurrences or exhaustive coverage of the requested literal scope; preserve it when using cursor.

query.description: Literal text to locate in canonical source, containing non-whitespace text and at most 4,096 Unicode scalar values. Exact mode preserves query whitespace; this is not a semantic question or regex. Read chosen hits using their start_lid/end_lid.

direction.description: before keeps hits ending at or before the reference span's start; after keeps hits starting at or after its end. Direction filters scope independently of result order.

resident.description: Answer a self-contained semantic question about explicit referents by resolving targets first and then reading source evidence around the frozen bindings.

obligations.requirement: State the activation condition at each location.
Compare whether equality activates each threshold, citing both passages.

examples.query: How do the activation conditions of the alpha threshold and beta threshold differ?

anchor_lid.description: Required known LID in this book anchoring referent resolution. It provides local context without restricting evidence retrieval to this node.

intent.description: Question kind: definition or explanation requires 1..3 targets; relation or comparison requires 2..3 separately named targets.

obligations.description: One to three answer requirements, each in its own requirement object; these guide evidence sufficiency for the requested answer.

requirement.description: One nonblank, independently checkable requirement the semantic answer must address.

query.description: Self-contained, nonblank semantic question about the named targets, with enough context to resolve referents. Use literal search for exact wording or first/previous occurrences.

targets.description: Explicit referents to resolve before reading evidence. Each item is nonblank and unique after trimming and lowercasing; name comparison/relation targets separately, not as one combined phrase.

resident.name: book.query

outputSchema.description: Resident delivered result. status/truncated describe the initial model delivery; candidate counts and query status inside model_body retain domain selection/support meaning. After sampling, the active-turn ledger can evict model_body to null while retaining the original status and receipt. Null never supplies fresh evidence. Receipt evidence lists only accepted delivered text.

context_cache.description: Bounded Resident prefetch and ready citations. Only delivered canonical text supplies source evidence; search excerpts and locators do not. Omitted text stays in the book with exact continuation calls.

citations.description: Ready citation IDs for the canonical text delivered by this read, bounded by its exact source_range. No omitted text is included.

end_lid.description: Inclusive final LID in source reading order; for a search hit, use end_lid. Reads from lid's span start through end_lid's span end. Omit or null to read only lid's span.

lid.description: Known LID from this book's locating or structure results; for a search hit, use start_lid. Reads the node's canonical source span, including descendants.

start_utf16.description: Absolute canonical-source UTF-16 position copied from a text continuation. Keep the original lid/end_lid. Omit or null for the initial read; a continuation returns a bounded page and its source_range, requested_range and next_start_utf16.

next_call.description: Optional source reads for a chosen locator; emitting a call does not observe its text.

cursor.description: Opaque next_cursor from the preceding search result. Omit or null for the first page; preserve query, match_mode, scope, order and page_size on continuation. A changed source revision invalidates it.

match_mode.description: exact (default) matches unchanged text; normalized applies NFKC, full non-Turkic case folding and whitespace collapsing. Both locate literal occurrences, not semantic equivalents; result ranges use original-source UTF-16 positions.

order.description: document (default) returns earliest occurrences first; reverse_document returns latest first. Uses canonical source order, not lexical LID sorting. Combine before with reverse_document for previous occurrences.

page_size.description: Maximum literal occurrences per search page, 1..50, default 20. Does not change total_occurrences or exhaustive coverage of the requested literal scope; preserve it when using cursor.

query.description: Literal text to locate in canonical source, containing non-whitespace text and at most 4,096 Unicode scalar values. Exact mode preserves query whitespace; this is not a semantic question or regex. Read chosen hits using their start_lid/end_lid.

direction.description: before keeps hits ending at or before the reference span's start; after keeps hits starting at or after its end. Direction filters scope independently of result order.

lid.description: Known reference LID in this book. The relative filter excludes this node's entire source span, including its descendants.

relative_to.description: Optional before/after filter around a known LID, excluding that node's span. Intersects with within_lid when both are supplied.

within_lid.description: Known LID whose source span, including descendants, must contain each whole hit. Omit or null for no subtree restriction.

scope.description: Optional source scope using known LIDs from this book. Omit, null or {} searches the whole book; within_lid and relative_to intersect, and each whole hit must fit the resulting range.

cursor.description: Opaque next_cursor from the preceding search result. Omit or null for the first page; preserve query, match_mode, scope, order and page_size on continuation. A changed source revision invalidates it.

match_mode.description: exact (default) matches unchanged text; normalized applies NFKC, full non-Turkic case folding and whitespace collapsing. Both locate literal occurrences, not semantic equivalents; result ranges use original-source UTF-16 positions.

order.description: document (default) returns earliest occurrences first; reverse_document returns latest first. Uses canonical source order, not lexical LID sorting. Combine before with reverse_document for previous occurrences.

page_size.description: Maximum literal occurrences per search page, 1..50, default 20. Does not change total_occurrences or exhaustive coverage of the requested literal scope; preserve it when using cursor.

query.description: Literal text to locate in canonical source, containing non-whitespace text and at most 4,096 Unicode scalar values. Exact mode preserves query whitespace; this is not a semantic question or regex. Read chosen hits using their start_lid/end_lid.

direction.description: before keeps hits ending at or before the reference span's start; after keeps hits starting at or after its end. Direction filters scope independently of result order.

lid.description: Known reference LID in this book. The relative filter excludes this node's entire source span, including its descendants.

relative_to.description: Optional before/after filter around a known LID, excluding that node's span. Intersects with within_lid when both are supplied.

within_lid.description: Known LID whose source span, including descendants, must contain each whole hit. Omit or null for no subtree restriction.

scope.description: Optional source scope using known LIDs from this book. Omit, null or {} searches the whole book; within_lid and relative_to intersect, and each whole hit must fit the resulting range.

cursor.description: Opaque next_cursor from the preceding search result. Omit or null for the first page; preserve query, match_mode, scope, order and page_size on continuation. A changed source revision invalidates it.

page_size.description: Maximum literal occurrences per search page, 1..50, default 20. Does not change total_occurrences or exhaustive coverage of the requested literal scope; preserve it when using cursor.

direction.description: before keeps hits ending at or before the reference span's start; after keeps hits starting at or after its end. Direction filters scope independently of result order.

lid.description: Known reference LID in this book. The relative filter excludes this node's entire source span, including its descendants.

relative_to.description: Optional before/after filter around a known LID, excluding that node's span. Intersects with within_lid when both are supplied.

scope.description: Optional source scope using known LIDs from this book. Omit, null or {} searches the whole book; within_lid and relative_to intersect, and each whole hit must fit the resulting range.

cursor.description: Opaque next_cursor from the preceding search result. Omit or null for the first page; preserve query, match_mode, scope, order and page_size on continuation. A changed source revision invalidates it.

cursor.description: Opaque next_cursor from the preceding search result. Omit or null for the first page; preserve query, match_mode, scope, order and page_size on continuation. A changed source revision invalidates it.

match_mode.description: exact (default) matches unchanged text; normalized applies NFKC, full non-Turkic case folding and whitespace collapsing. Both locate literal occurrences, not semantic equivalents; result ranges use original-source UTF-16 positions.

order.description: document (default) returns earliest occurrences first; reverse_document returns latest first. Uses canonical source order, not lexical LID sorting. Combine before with reverse_document for previous occurrences.

page_size.description: Maximum literal occurrences per search page, 1..50, default 20. Does not change total_occurrences or exhaustive coverage of the requested literal scope; preserve it when using cursor.

query.description: Literal text to locate in canonical source, containing non-whitespace text and at most 4,096 Unicode scalar values. Exact mode preserves query whitespace; this is not a semantic question or regex. Read chosen hits using their start_lid/end_lid.

direction.description: before keeps hits ending at or before the reference span's start; after keeps hits starting at or after its end. Direction filters scope independently of result order.

cursor.description: Opaque next_cursor from the preceding search result. Omit or null for the first page; preserve query, match_mode, scope, order and page_size on continuation. A changed source revision invalidates it.

match_mode.description: exact (default) matches unchanged text; normalized applies NFKC, full non-Turkic case folding and whitespace collapsing. Both locate literal occurrences, not semantic equivalents; result ranges use original-source UTF-16 positions.

order.description: document (default) returns earliest occurrences first; reverse_document returns latest first. Uses canonical source order, not lexical LID sorting. Combine before with reverse_document for previous occurrences.

page_size.description: Maximum literal occurrences per search page, 1..50, default 20. Does not change total_occurrences or exhaustive coverage of the requested literal scope; preserve it when using cursor.

query.description: Literal text to locate in canonical source, containing non-whitespace text and at most 4,096 Unicode scalar values. Exact mode preserves query whitespace; this is not a semantic question or regex. Read chosen hits using their start_lid/end_lid.

direction.description: before keeps hits ending at or before the reference span's start; after keeps hits starting at or after its end. Direction filters scope independently of result order.

within_lid.description: Known LID whose source span, including descendants, must contain each whole hit. Omit or null for no subtree restriction.

resident.description: Read several known source ranges together, preserving each range separately. For a continuous argument, sequence or case, use its known lid and end_lid to read the complete relevant relationship, not just isolated matching sentences or titles. Locate only missing endpoints with context or search before reading; never guess LIDs. Prefer one batch for independent ranges; use book.text for a single range. Only delivered text is evidence; follow next_start_utf16 when the needed scope continues beyond the returned text.

resident.description: Update the active Resident task only when interpretation, requirements or working state changes. working saves concise results in focus, remaining knowledge or understanding gaps in open_questions, the next concrete action in next_move, and optionally replaces the plan; refine sets interpretation/requirements only in the goal's origin turn; revise changes requirements using the current user turn ID and an exact quote from that message. Replace example turn IDs with actual IDs from the active Goal; each requirement must cite the origin or current user turn. Working items record a revisable plan, not user requirements. Keep the plan consistent with actual results and remaining content gaps before finishing. Success returns {goal_id, revision, changed}; changed=false means no state change. This tool cannot mark delivery or Goal completion; completed items do not prove either. Short direct answers need no update or plan. Use working in a separate call to save focus, next_move or plan items; refine/revise do not accept these fields.

focus.description: Optional kind of original passage to locate using the book's concept and discourse index.

limit.description: Maximum ranked candidate passages, 1..20; omit or null for 8. Scores rank candidates and are not confidence. A bounded result cannot establish semantic exhaustiveness.

query.description: Nonblank natural-language question or terms to find relevant canonical-source passages. Ranking is lexical; translated or synonymous terms can help when the original wording differs.

cursor.description: Opaque next_cursor from the preceding search result. Omit or null for the first page; preserve query, match_mode, scope, order and page_size on continuation. A changed source revision invalidates it.

match_mode.description: exact (default) matches unchanged text; normalized applies NFKC, full non-Turkic case folding and whitespace collapsing. Both locate literal occurrences, not semantic equivalents; result ranges use original-source UTF-16 positions.

order.description: document (default) returns earliest occurrences first; reverse_document returns latest first. Uses canonical source order, not lexical LID sorting. Combine before with reverse_document for previous occurrences.

page_size.description: Maximum literal occurrences per search page, 1..50, default 20. Does not change total_occurrences or exhaustive coverage of the requested literal scope; preserve it when using cursor.

query.description: Literal text to locate in canonical source, containing non-whitespace text and at most 4,096 Unicode scalar values. Exact mode preserves query whitespace; this is not a semantic question or regex. Read chosen hits using their start_lid/end_lid.

direction.description: before keeps hits ending at or before the reference span's start; after keeps hits starting at or after its end. Direction filters scope independently of result order.

lid.description: Known reference LID in this book. The relative filter excludes this node's entire source span, including its descendants.

relative_to.description: Optional before/after filter around a known LID, excluding that node's span. Intersects with within_lid when both are supplied.

within_lid.description: Known LID whose source span, including descendants, must contain each whole hit. Omit or null for no subtree restriction.

scope.description: Optional source scope using known LIDs from this book. Omit, null or {} searches the whole book; within_lid and relative_to intersect, and each whole hit must fit the resulting range.

anchor_lid.description: Optional known LID in this book to rank nearby candidates and previews. Omit or null for unanchored ranking; this does not restrict recall to a subtree.

focus.description: Optional kind of source passage to locate for this concept.

limit.description: Maximum concept/entity candidates, 1..50; omit or null for 12. Inspect matched_count and truncated for candidate coverage; this does not limit occurrences within a candidate.

query.description: Nonblank concept/entity name, alias or descriptive terms for deterministic candidate recall from names and occurrence text. At most 4,096 Unicode scalar values, including surrounding whitespace; not literal occurrence enumeration.

at.description: Optional known LID in this book to locate its structural role or current route segment. Omit or null for the whole-book view; this is a location, not a natural-language query.

granularity.description: Context reach: near includes tree adjacency and local relations; mid adds other concept/entity occurrences; far also adds long-range relations. Omit or null for near.

k.description: Maximum number of context pointers returned across all layers. Omit or null for 10; zero returns no items. total_candidates counts deduplicated pointers before k; returned_count and truncated describe selection by k before pagination or output budgeting. Counts pointers, not distinct LIDs, characters or source passages.

resident.description: Register playable examples and computed score facts. Read both endpoints with music.read first. kind=score selects one part/voice from from_id through through_id inclusive, retaining intervening notes, chords, ties and rests (at most 200 objects). It returns a listen marker and facts_marker. Insert facts_marker as a standalone paragraph to display host-computed pitches, durations and endpoint span verbatim; explain their significance in your prose. kind=comparison takes left/right selections and returns both playable examples plus one facts_marker with both passages and an onset/rhythm/pitch comparison. If rhythmic structures differ, choose explicit corresponding subranges instead of assuming note correspondence. A constant pitch-class shift may still involve different octave changes. These calculations do not establish thematic derivation. Batch a few short passages per call. kind=illustration makes an explicitly invented example from pitch names with octaves and quarter-note durations; empty pitches is rest. Insert listen markers inline where the sound belongs. Registration never starts playback; the fixed piano tempo is quarter=66 and tremolo strokes are not expanded.

Catalog/event query terms match independently and are ranked. Score note_pairs gives computed written intervals and duration ratios; notation retains visibility, spelling and playback dynamics. Events supports query/event_id/range/part filters; score returns notes, key/time signatures, tempo/direction marks, inherited notation context and alignment including separate repeated occurrences. Score query also searches mark text, such as Allegro. Raw encoded_mode and MusicXML playback tempo remain distinct from reviewed work_tonality and measured recording tempo. Score facts are usable independently of audio-alignment coverage. Score pages preserve complete part/voice measures. Select a single voice and a short range, normally limit=64; inspect returned_scope and range_complete, and follow next_offset when present. Explicit source_ids/query matches may be partial measures. Use music.example for complete passage facts and comparisons. Copy sources[].target into source.present music_target to cite the read snapshot, including its notation facts and tonality provenance. The input-time music question remains fixed when playback advances.

move.delivery_text: Whole-trip average speed is distance divided by all elapsed time. Both the time moving and the time stopped belong to that elapsed time. For 10 km with 10 minutes moving and 5 stopped, that means dividing 10 km by 15 minutes.
move.explanation: Total elapsed time rises from 15 to 18 minutes while the 10 km distance stays fixed, so whole-trip average speed falls.
move.hint: Keep the 10 km numerator fixed and compare total elapsed time.

participation.learner_inference: Whether a longer stop changes whole-trip average speed when distance and moving time stay fixed.

response_expectation.public_prompt: For the same 10 km journey, keep moving time fixed at 10 minutes and change only the stop from 5 to 8 minutes. Would whole-trip average speed rise, fall or stay the same? What changed in the relationship?

items.criterion: Rejects A's claim: A's total journey time includes the stop, giving 15 minutes versus B's 12; for the same distance, B has the greater average speed. Equivalent wording or time units are accepted; numerical speed calculations may be omitted. Repeating the definition without applying it to these journeys is insufficient.

move.delivery_text: Whole-trip average speed is distance divided by all elapsed time, including stops. A and B each travel 10 km. A takes 10 minutes moving and stops for 5 minutes; B takes 12 minutes without stopping. A says, 'I moved faster, so my average speed for the whole trip was higher.' Is that claim correct? Explain using both journeys.
move.explanation: For the whole trip, average speed uses total distance divided by all elapsed time. A takes 10 + 5 = 15 minutes and B takes 12; over the same 10 km, B has the greater whole-trip average speed. Excluding the stop gives A's moving-only average speed; that answers a different question and cannot support A's whole-trip claim.

participation.learner_inference: Whether faster movement alone establishes a higher whole-trip average speed for these two journeys.
participation.reason: A comparison can distinguish moving-only speed from the whole-trip relationship after its premises are available.
participation.support: Supply average speed as distance divided by all elapsed time; the prompt supplies equal distances, moving times and the stop.

move.delivery_text: Draw two columns on paper: distance and elapsed time. For a 10 km ride lasting 10 minutes, put 10 km and 10 minutes on the first row. For a 5 minute stop, put 0 km and 5 minutes on the next row. Add each column: this journey covers 10 km in 15 minutes, including the stop. These totals supply the distance and time for average speed.

participation.reason: The current obstacle is how to start the table; supply a usable method without diagnosing a conceptual error.
participation.support: Place each interval's distance and time on the same row, include the stop, then add each column.

move.delivery_text: Compare plans using the same route distance and all elapsed time, including stops. Shorter stops can reduce total time; faster movement can also reduce it when road and safety conditions permit. Preserve any necessary rest stops. List moving time, stopped time and feasibility for each plan, then explain which constraints make a plan useful. Both changes may be combined; the average-speed relationship alone does not choose a unique plan.

participation.reason: The learner asks for open plan analysis, so supply comparison criteria and reasons before requesting a decision.
participation.support: Compare total times and feasibility under the same distance and accepted constraints; retain multiple justified choices.

move.prompt: Give a framework for comparing travel plans under the learner's constraints; several plans may be reasonable.

target.expected_performance: Connect the stopped interval to the elapsed time of this same whole journey.

move.delivery_text: Define the average speed as the constant speed that would cover the same total distance d during the same elapsed time T. A constant speed v covers vT, so matching this journey gives vT = d. With T positive, dividing both sides by T gives v = d/T. In the earlier 10 km journey, 10 minutes moving plus 5 stopped gives T = 15 minutes = 0.25 hours, so the whole-trip average is 10/0.25 = 40 km/h. The stop belongs to that elapsed interval even though it adds no distance.

blocks.purpose: Distinguish whole-journey average speed from moving-only speed.
blocks.relation: Using the source definition, which intervals belong to the elapsed time of the whole journey?

design.organizing_model: Use the source definition to compare two equal-distance journeys, then examine which elapsed intervals belong in each denominator.

representation.reason: One concrete journey and its stop make the missing time relationship usable in a short comparison.

design.revision_reason: Initial design for the learner's current request.

target.expected_performance: Explain why total time is the denominator

edits.new_text: All elapsed journey time, including the stop, belongs in the denominator. For the same 10 km journey, 10 minutes moving and 5 minutes stopped give 15 minutes in total, so the whole-journey average speed is 40 km/h.

participation.reason: The requested explanation is complete; remove the unintended new task.

move.delivery_text: Picture the journey from departure to arrival: 10 minutes moving, then 5 minutes stopped before you arrive. The clock for this whole journey keeps running during the stop. Its elapsed time is therefore 15 minutes. That is the time used for this journey's average speed.

participation.learner_inference: Use that time boundary to decide whether a longer stop changes the whole-trip average when distance stays fixed.
participation.reason: The learner has not yet connected whole-trip time to time spent stopped; provide that connection first.
participation.support: The journey begins on departure and ends on arrival, so its elapsed time includes the stop.

move.prompt: Follow one journey on a timeline: 10 minutes moving and then 5 minutes stopped before arrival. Show that both intervals belong to this same journey. Establish that connection here without also introducing comparisons between journeys.

target.expected_performance: Connect the stopped interval to the elapsed time of this same whole journey.

move.delivery_text: Picture the journey from departure to arrival: 10 minutes moving, then 5 minutes stopped before you arrive. The clock for this whole journey keeps running during the stop. Its elapsed time is therefore 15 minutes. That is the time used for this journey's average speed.

participation.learner_inference: How the learner describes the stop's place in the whole journey, using the explained timeline.
participation.reason: Hearing how the learner connects the stop to the journey can reveal which part of this supplied explanation needs further help.
participation.support: The timeline runs from departure to arrival and includes both the moving interval and the stopped interval.

move.prompt: Complete the explanation of this journey's elapsed time, then invite the learner's own account of that connection. Their expression can guide the next help without claiming independent application.

response_expectation.public_prompt: In your own words, why does the stopped part still belong to the time for this whole journey? You can use the timeline above.

target.expected_performance: Express how the stopped interval belongs to this journey, with the supplied timeline available.

move.delivery_text: Whole-trip average speed is distance divided by all elapsed time. Both the time moving and the time stopped belong to that elapsed time. For 10 km with 10 minutes moving and 5 stopped, that means dividing 10 km by 15 minutes.
move.explanation: Total elapsed time rises from 15 to 18 minutes while the 10 km distance stays fixed, so whole-trip average speed falls.
move.hint: Keep the 10 km numerator fixed and compare total elapsed time.

participation.learner_inference: Whether a longer stop changes whole-trip average speed when distance and moving time stay fixed.
participation.reason: The learner can use the supplied whole-trip relationship to judge a changed stop, making the uncertain time connection visible.
participation.support: First supply total distance divided by all elapsed time, and identify moving and stopped time as parts of that elapsed time.

move.prompt: Make clear that whole-trip time includes moving and stopped time. Leave the learner to decide what happens to average speed when the same journey has a longer stop.

response_expectation.public_prompt: For the same 10 km journey, keep moving time fixed at 10 minutes and change only the stop from 5 to 8 minutes. Would whole-trip average speed rise, fall or stay the same? What changed in the relationship?

target.expected_performance: Use the supplied whole-trip time relationship to predict average speed when only the stop becomes longer.

items.criterion: Rejects A's claim: A's total journey time includes the stop, giving 15 minutes versus B's 12; for the same distance, B has the greater average speed. Equivalent wording or time units are accepted; numerical speed calculations may be omitted. Repeating the definition without applying it to these journeys is insufficient.

move.delivery_text: Whole-trip average speed is distance divided by all elapsed time, including stops. A and B each travel 10 km. A takes 10 minutes moving and stops for 5 minutes; B takes 12 minutes without stopping. A says, 'I moved faster, so my average speed for the whole trip was higher.' Is that claim correct? Explain using both journeys.
move.explanation: For the whole trip, average speed uses total distance divided by all elapsed time. A takes 10 + 5 = 15 minutes and B takes 12; over the same 10 km, B has the greater whole-trip average speed. Excluding the stop gives A's moving-only average speed; that answers a different question and cannot support A's whole-trip claim.

participation.learner_inference: Whether faster movement alone establishes a higher whole-trip average speed for these two journeys.
participation.reason: A comparison can distinguish moving-only speed from the whole-trip relationship after its premises are available.
participation.support: Supply average speed as distance divided by all elapsed time; the prompt supplies equal distances, moving times and the stop.

move.prompt: A and B each travel 10 km. A takes 10 minutes moving and stops for 5 minutes; B takes 12 minutes without stopping. A says, 'I moved faster, so my average speed for the whole trip was higher.' Is that claim correct? Explain using both journeys.

target.expected_performance: Use total elapsed time, including a stop, to judge whether higher moving speed implies higher whole-trip average speed for equal-distance journeys.

move.delivery_text: You connected the stop to the time of this whole journey: the journey has not ended while the traveler is stopped, so that interval belongs in its elapsed time. That explains the denominator in this example.

participation.reason: The learner has already supplied the relevant relationship and reason for the current example; no further attempt is needed for this request.

move.prompt: Acknowledge the learner's stated connection between the stop and whole-trip time in this example, without claiming wider independent application.

target.expected_performance: Connect the stopped interval to the elapsed time of this same whole journey.

move.delivery_text: Draw two columns on paper: distance and elapsed time. For a 10 km ride lasting 10 minutes, put 10 km and 10 minutes on the first row. For a 5 minute stop, put 0 km and 5 minutes on the next row. Add each column: this journey covers 10 km in 15 minutes, including the stop. These totals supply the distance and time for average speed.

participation.reason: The current obstacle is how to start the table; supply a usable method without diagnosing a conceptual error.
participation.support: Place each interval's distance and time on the same row, include the stop, then add each column.

move.prompt: Help the learner start a paper journey table before asking them to compare journeys.

target.expected_performance: Connect the stopped interval to the elapsed time of this same whole journey.

move.delivery_text: Compare plans using the same route distance and all elapsed time, including stops. Shorter stops can reduce total time; faster movement can also reduce it when road and safety conditions permit. Preserve any necessary rest stops. List moving time, stopped time and feasibility for each plan, then explain which constraints make a plan useful. Both changes may be combined; the average-speed relationship alone does not choose a unique plan.

participation.reason: The learner asks for open plan analysis, so supply comparison criteria and reasons before requesting a decision.
participation.support: Compare total times and feasibility under the same distance and accepted constraints; retain multiple justified choices.

move.prompt: Give a framework for comparing travel plans under the learner's constraints; several plans may be reasonable.

target.expected_performance: Connect the stopped interval to the elapsed time of this same whole journey.

move.delivery_text: Define the average speed as the constant speed that would cover the same total distance d during the same elapsed time T. A constant speed v covers vT, so matching this journey gives vT = d. With T positive, dividing both sides by T gives v = d/T. In the earlier 10 km journey, 10 minutes moving plus 5 stopped gives T = 15 minutes = 0.25 hours, so the whole-trip average is 10/0.25 = 40 km/h. The stop belongs to that elapsed interval even though it adds no distance.
move.intent_quote: This time, derive the formula directly using the previous journey.

participation.reason: The current explicit request asks for the full derivation with the previous example; complete it without a preliminary test or a new invitation.

move.prompt: Use the earlier journey to derive the whole-trip average-speed formula at the requested depth, even if an earlier preference favored simple examples.

target.expected_performance: Connect the stopped interval to the elapsed time of this same whole journey.

move.delivery_text: Picture the journey from departure to arrival: 10 minutes moving, then 5 minutes stopped before you arrive. The clock for this whole journey keeps running during the stop. Its elapsed time is therefore 15 minutes. That is the time used for this journey's average speed.

move.delivery_text: Picture the journey from departure to arrival: 10 minutes moving, then 5 minutes stopped before you arrive. The clock for this whole journey keeps running during the stop. Its elapsed time is therefore 15 minutes. That is the time used for this journey's average speed.

participation.learner_inference: How the learner describes the stop's place in the whole journey, using the explained timeline.
participation.reason: Hearing how the learner connects the stop to the journey can reveal which part of this supplied explanation needs further help.
participation.support: The timeline runs from departure to arrival and includes both the moving interval and the stopped interval.

move.prompt: Complete the explanation of this journey's elapsed time, then invite the learner's own account of that connection. Their expression can guide the next help without claiming independent application.

response_expectation.public_prompt: In your own words, why does the stopped part still belong to the time for this whole journey? You can use the timeline above.

target.expected_performance: Express how the stopped interval belongs to this journey, with the supplied timeline available.

move.delivery_text: Whole-trip average speed is distance divided by all elapsed time. Both the time moving and the time stopped belong to that elapsed time. For 10 km with 10 minutes moving and 5 stopped, that means dividing 10 km by 15 minutes.
move.explanation: Total elapsed time rises from 15 to 18 minutes while the 10 km distance stays fixed, so whole-trip average speed falls.
move.hint: Keep the 10 km numerator fixed and compare total elapsed time.

participation.learner_inference: Whether a longer stop changes whole-trip average speed when distance and moving time stay fixed.
participation.reason: The learner can use the supplied whole-trip relationship to judge a changed stop, making the uncertain time connection visible.
participation.support: First supply total distance divided by all elapsed time, and identify moving and stopped time as parts of that elapsed time.

move.prompt: Make clear that whole-trip time includes moving and stopped time. Leave the learner to decide what happens to average speed when the same journey has a longer stop.

response_expectation.public_prompt: For the same 10 km journey, keep moving time fixed at 10 minutes and change only the stop from 5 to 8 minutes. Would whole-trip average speed rise, fall or stay the same? What changed in the relationship?

target.expected_performance: Use the supplied whole-trip time relationship to predict average speed when only the stop becomes longer.

items.criterion: Rejects A's claim: A's total journey time includes the stop, giving 15 minutes versus B's 12; for the same distance, B has the greater average speed. Equivalent wording or time units are accepted; numerical speed calculations may be omitted. Repeating the definition without applying it to these journeys is insufficient.

move.delivery_text: Whole-trip average speed is distance divided by all elapsed time, including stops. A and B each travel 10 km. A takes 10 minutes moving and stops for 5 minutes; B takes 12 minutes without stopping. A says, 'I moved faster, so my average speed for the whole trip was higher.' Is that claim correct? Explain using both journeys.
move.explanation: For the whole trip, average speed uses total distance divided by all elapsed time. A takes 10 + 5 = 15 minutes and B takes 12; over the same 10 km, B has the greater whole-trip average speed. Excluding the stop gives A's moving-only average speed; that answers a different question and cannot support A's whole-trip claim.

participation.learner_inference: Whether faster movement alone establishes a higher whole-trip average speed for these two journeys.
participation.reason: A comparison can distinguish moving-only speed from the whole-trip relationship after its premises are available.
participation.support: Supply average speed as distance divided by all elapsed time; the prompt supplies equal distances, moving times and the stop.

move.prompt: A and B each travel 10 km. A takes 10 minutes moving and stops for 5 minutes; B takes 12 minutes without stopping. A says, 'I moved faster, so my average speed for the whole trip was higher.' Is that claim correct? Explain using both journeys.

target.expected_performance: Use total elapsed time, including a stop, to judge whether higher moving speed implies higher whole-trip average speed for equal-distance journeys.

move.delivery_text: You connected the stop to the time of this whole journey: the journey has not ended while the traveler is stopped, so that interval belongs in its elapsed time. That explains the denominator in this example.

participation.reason: The learner has already supplied the relevant relationship and reason for the current example; no further attempt is needed for this request.

move.prompt: Acknowledge the learner's stated connection between the stop and whole-trip time in this example, without claiming wider independent application.

target.expected_performance: Connect the stopped interval to the elapsed time of this same whole journey.

move.delivery_text: Draw two columns on paper: distance and elapsed time. For a 10 km ride lasting 10 minutes, put 10 km and 10 minutes on the first row. For a 5 minute stop, put 0 km and 5 minutes on the next row. Add each column: this journey covers 10 km in 15 minutes, including the stop. These totals supply the distance and time for average speed.

participation.reason: The current obstacle is how to start the table; supply a usable method without diagnosing a conceptual error.
participation.support: Place each interval's distance and time on the same row, include the stop, then add each column.

move.prompt: Help the learner start a paper journey table before asking them to compare journeys.

target.expected_performance: Connect the stopped interval to the elapsed time of this same whole journey.

move.delivery_text: Compare plans using the same route distance and all elapsed time, including stops. Shorter stops can reduce total time; faster movement can also reduce it when road and safety conditions permit. Preserve any necessary rest stops. List moving time, stopped time and feasibility for each plan, then explain which constraints make a plan useful. Both changes may be combined; the average-speed relationship alone does not choose a unique plan.

participation.reason: The learner asks for open plan analysis, so supply comparison criteria and reasons before requesting a decision.
participation.support: Compare total times and feasibility under the same distance and accepted constraints; retain multiple justified choices.

move.prompt: Give a framework for comparing travel plans under the learner's constraints; several plans may be reasonable.

target.expected_performance: Connect the stopped interval to the elapsed time of this same whole journey.

move.delivery_text: Define the average speed as the constant speed that would cover the same total distance d during the same elapsed time T. A constant speed v covers vT, so matching this journey gives vT = d. With T positive, dividing both sides by T gives v = d/T. In the earlier 10 km journey, 10 minutes moving plus 5 stopped gives T = 15 minutes = 0.25 hours, so the whole-trip average is 10/0.25 = 40 km/h. The stop belongs to that elapsed interval even though it adds no distance.
move.intent_quote: This time, derive the formula directly using the previous journey.

participation.reason: The current explicit request asks for the full derivation with the previous example; complete it without a preliminary test or a new invitation.

move.prompt: Use the earlier journey to derive the whole-trip average-speed formula at the requested depth, even if an earlier preference favored simple examples.

target.expected_performance: Connect the stopped interval to the elapsed time of this same whole journey.

blocks.purpose: Distinguish whole-journey average speed from moving-only speed.
blocks.relation: Using the source definition, which intervals belong to the elapsed time of the whole journey?

design.organizing_model: Use the source definition to compare two equal-distance journeys, then examine which elapsed intervals belong in each denominator.

representation.reason: One concrete journey and its stop make the missing time relationship usable in a short comparison.

design.revision_reason: Initial design for the learner's current request.

target.expected_performance: Explain why total time is the denominator

edits.new_text: All elapsed journey time, including the stop, belongs in the denominator. For the same 10 km journey, 10 minutes moving and 5 minutes stopped give 15 minutes in total, so the whole-journey average speed is 40 km/h.

participation.reason: The requested explanation is complete; remove the unintended new task.

move.delivery_text: Picture the journey from departure to arrival: 10 minutes moving, then 5 minutes stopped before you arrive. The clock for this whole journey keeps running during the stop. Its elapsed time is therefore 15 minutes. That is the time used for this journey's average speed.

participation.learner_inference: Use that time boundary to decide whether a longer stop changes the whole-trip average when distance stays fixed.
participation.reason: The learner has not yet connected whole-trip time to time spent stopped; provide that connection first.
participation.support: The journey begins on departure and ends on arrival, so its elapsed time includes the stop.

move.prompt: Follow one journey on a timeline: 10 minutes moving and then 5 minutes stopped before arrival. Show that both intervals belong to this same journey. Establish that connection here without also introducing comparisons between journeys.

target.expected_performance: Connect the stopped interval to the elapsed time of this same whole journey.

move.delivery_text: Picture the journey from departure to arrival: 10 minutes moving, then 5 minutes stopped before you arrive. The clock for this whole journey keeps running during the stop. Its elapsed time is therefore 15 minutes. That is the time used for this journey's average speed.

participation.learner_inference: How the learner describes the stop's place in the whole journey, using the explained timeline.
participation.reason: Hearing how the learner connects the stop to the journey can reveal which part of this supplied explanation needs further help.
participation.support: The timeline runs from departure to arrival and includes both the moving interval and the stopped interval.

move.prompt: Complete the explanation of this journey's elapsed time, then invite the learner's own account of that connection. Their expression can guide the next help without claiming independent application.

response_expectation.public_prompt: In your own words, why does the stopped part still belong to the time for this whole journey? You can use the timeline above.

target.expected_performance: Express how the stopped interval belongs to this journey, with the supplied timeline available.

move.delivery_text: Whole-trip average speed is distance divided by all elapsed time. Both the time moving and the time stopped belong to that elapsed time. For 10 km with 10 minutes moving and 5 stopped, that means dividing 10 km by 15 minutes.
move.explanation: Total elapsed time rises from 15 to 18 minutes while the 10 km distance stays fixed, so whole-trip average speed falls.
move.hint: Keep the 10 km numerator fixed and compare total elapsed time.

participation.learner_inference: Whether a longer stop changes whole-trip average speed when distance and moving time stay fixed.
participation.reason: The learner can use the supplied whole-trip relationship to judge a changed stop, making the uncertain time connection visible.
participation.support: First supply total distance divided by all elapsed time, and identify moving and stopped time as parts of that elapsed time.

move.prompt: Make clear that whole-trip time includes moving and stopped time. Leave the learner to decide what happens to average speed when the same journey has a longer stop.

response_expectation.public_prompt: For the same 10 km journey, keep moving time fixed at 10 minutes and change only the stop from 5 to 8 minutes. Would whole-trip average speed rise, fall or stay the same? What changed in the relationship?

target.expected_performance: Use the supplied whole-trip time relationship to predict average speed when only the stop becomes longer.

items.criterion: Rejects A's claim: A's total journey time includes the stop, giving 15 minutes versus B's 12; for the same distance, B has the greater average speed. Equivalent wording or time units are accepted; numerical speed calculations may be omitted. Repeating the definition without applying it to these journeys is insufficient.

move.delivery_text: Whole-trip average speed is distance divided by all elapsed time, including stops. A and B each travel 10 km. A takes 10 minutes moving and stops for 5 minutes; B takes 12 minutes without stopping. A says, 'I moved faster, so my average speed for the whole trip was higher.' Is that claim correct? Explain using both journeys.
move.explanation: For the whole trip, average speed uses total distance divided by all elapsed time. A takes 10 + 5 = 15 minutes and B takes 12; over the same 10 km, B has the greater whole-trip average speed. Excluding the stop gives A's moving-only average speed; that answers a different question and cannot support A's whole-trip claim.

participation.learner_inference: Whether faster movement alone establishes a higher whole-trip average speed for these two journeys.
participation.reason: A comparison can distinguish moving-only speed from the whole-trip relationship after its premises are available.
participation.support: Supply average speed as distance divided by all elapsed time; the prompt supplies equal distances, moving times and the stop.

move.prompt: A and B each travel 10 km. A takes 10 minutes moving and stops for 5 minutes; B takes 12 minutes without stopping. A says, 'I moved faster, so my average speed for the whole trip was higher.' Is that claim correct? Explain using both journeys.

target.expected_performance: Use total elapsed time, including a stop, to judge whether higher moving speed implies higher whole-trip average speed for equal-distance journeys.

move.delivery_text: You connected the stop to the time of this whole journey: the journey has not ended while the traveler is stopped, so that interval belongs in its elapsed time. That explains the denominator in this example.

participation.reason: The learner has already supplied the relevant relationship and reason for the current example; no further attempt is needed for this request.

move.prompt: Acknowledge the learner's stated connection between the stop and whole-trip time in this example, without claiming wider independent application.

target.expected_performance: Connect the stopped interval to the elapsed time of this same whole journey.

move.delivery_text: Draw two columns on paper: distance and elapsed time. For a 10 km ride lasting 10 minutes, put 10 km and 10 minutes on the first row. For a 5 minute stop, put 0 km and 5 minutes on the next row. Add each column: this journey covers 10 km in 15 minutes, including the stop. These totals supply the distance and time for average speed.

participation.reason: The current obstacle is how to start the table; supply a usable method without diagnosing a conceptual error.
participation.support: Place each interval's distance and time on the same row, include the stop, then add each column.

move.prompt: Help the learner start a paper journey table before asking them to compare journeys.

target.expected_performance: Connect the stopped interval to the elapsed time of this same whole journey.

move.delivery_text: Compare plans using the same route distance and all elapsed time, including stops. Shorter stops can reduce total time; faster movement can also reduce it when road and safety conditions permit. Preserve any necessary rest stops. List moving time, stopped time and feasibility for each plan, then explain which constraints make a plan useful. Both changes may be combined; the average-speed relationship alone does not choose a unique plan.

participation.reason: The learner asks for open plan analysis, so supply comparison criteria and reasons before requesting a decision.
participation.support: Compare total times and feasibility under the same distance and accepted constraints; retain multiple justified choices.

move.prompt: Give a framework for comparing travel plans under the learner's constraints; several plans may be reasonable.

target.expected_performance: Connect the stopped interval to the elapsed time of this same whole journey.

move.delivery_text: Define the average speed as the constant speed that would cover the same total distance d during the same elapsed time T. A constant speed v covers vT, so matching this journey gives vT = d. With T positive, dividing both sides by T gives v = d/T. In the earlier 10 km journey, 10 minutes moving plus 5 stopped gives T = 15 minutes = 0.25 hours, so the whole-trip average is 10/0.25 = 40 km/h. The stop belongs to that elapsed interval even though it adds no distance.
move.intent_quote: This time, derive the formula directly using the previous journey.

participation.reason: The current explicit request asks for the full derivation with the previous example; complete it without a preliminary test or a new invitation.

move.prompt: Use the earlier journey to derive the whole-trip average-speed formula at the requested depth, even if an earlier preference favored simple examples.

target.expected_performance: Connect the stopped interval to the elapsed time of this same whole journey.

spec.description: Select one source-grounded move after reading original text, video transcript/frames/audio review, or prepared music with music.read this turn.
